argument: Leibniz, like Spinoza, holds there is only one kind of substance, but where Spinoza's substance is the totality of everything, Leibniz's is the smallest possible unit — the monad, a simple, non-physical thing that cannot be subdivided because it has no extension. Monads are windowless, meaning nothing ever passes directly between them; instead, each one contains from creation a complete script of its relationship to every other monad across all of time, a state Leibniz calls preestablished harmony, which is why they appear coordinated without ever interacting. This metaphysics underwrites Leibniz's distinction between two kinds of truth: truths of reasoning, which are necessarily true by definition alone (like 'all bachelors are unmarried'), and truths of fact, which are only contingently true and can mislead us if we generalize from limited observation (the mansion with the lights on) — a distinction that will matter directly for his theodicy in the next episode.
keyIdeas: The BuyPhone/iPhone story illustrates that two people can independently arrive at the same landmark discovery without wrongdoing — the same situation, the episode argues, as Leibniz and Newton both independently developing calculus.

Leibniz agrees with Spinoza that there is only one true substance, but disagrees on what it is: Spinoza's one substance is everything in the universe taken as a totality, while Leibniz's is the smallest possible unit, so small it isn't physical at all — the monad.

Anything with extension (taking up physical space) can in principle be bisected into smaller, interdependent parts, so it can't be the simplest, self-explaining thing that exists — which is why a true substance must be non-physical, unlike an atom.

Monads 'have no windows': nothing passes into or out of them, and there is no direct interaction (secondary causation) between them — each already contains everything it will ever be from the moment of creation, coordinated through preestablished harmony rather than real-time interaction.

Leibniz distinguishes truths of reasoning (necessarily true by the definition of their terms, like 'all bachelors are unmarried') from truths of fact (contingently true, based on observation, and prone to mistaken generalization, as in the mansion-with-the-lights-on example).

terms.def: Leibniz's single true substance: a simple, non-physical, indivisible unit that everything in the universe is ultimately made up of.
The property of taking up physical space (length, breadth, depth); anything with extension can in principle be subdivided, so it can't qualify as Leibniz's simplest substance.
Leibniz's claim that nothing passes directly into or out of a monad — no monad ever causally interacts with another.

The state in which each monad contains, from creation, a complete script of its relationship to every other monad across all of time, so that they appear coordinated without ever directly interacting.
